facts: President Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Miller previously served as deputy chief of staff and has been a chief architect of Trump's immigration policies, including mass deportation efforts and revoking temporary protected status for immigrants from countries such as Somalia and Haiti.

ladder.analysis:
Trump's decision to elevate Stephen Miller from deputy to chief of staff marks a notable shift in tone after a midterm cycle in which voter data suggested immigration enforcement contributed to Democratic gains. The move replaces Susie Wiles, who was widely viewed as a stabilizing presence, with someone associated with confrontation rather than compromise, raising questions about how the White House will operate as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January.

The change comes as Congress faces a hard Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government, with Republicans holding only a narrow House majority and a limited window to confirm judicial and executive nominees before losing control. The juxtaposition of Trump's own mixed signals—publicly suggesting deportation policy went 'too tough' while installing its chief advocate as chief of staff—adds uncertainty about the administration's direction heading into a politically weakened second half of the term.
ladder.steelman: The appointment itself is a clear, verifiable signal of strategic intent, but Trump's own contradictory public statements—calling deportation policy possibly 'too tough' while promoting its architect to the top staff job—show that interpreting his next moves requires separating stated intent from action.
ladder.implications: With Miller now serving as chief of staff, expect continued emphasis on immigration enforcement and executive authority, even as the administration faces a newly empowered Democratic Congress in January. The coming weeks will test whether the government funding deadline, judicial confirmations, and any further staffing moves reinforce a more confrontational governing posture or prompt further recalibration.

The decision was unsigned (per curiam); Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only noted dissenter and did not explain her reasoning.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone had invalidated the waivers on Oct. 2, 2026, ruling the secretary lacked such sweeping authority, and declined to stay her own ruling, prompting the administration's appeal to the Supreme Court.

Government data cited in the case shows the Big Bend region had 1.3% of total U.S. border apprehensions in 2025, and apprehensions within Big Bend National Park itself accounted for 0.045% of the national total; the administration separately cites about 89,000 detentions in the broader region in recent years.
ladder.analysis: The ruling is a procedural win for the Trump administration in an ongoing legal fight over how far federal agencies can go in waiving environmental and preservation laws to build border infrastructure. It does not resolve the core legal question — whether a 1996 statute permitting waivers in areas of 'high illegal entry' can be applied across a 517-mile stretch that, by the government's own data, sees comparatively few crossings — but it lets construction proceed while that question is litigated. The case highlights a recurring tension in border-wall disputes: the breadth of executive waiver authority versus the scope of judicial review, with the Supreme Court here signaling skepticism of the district court's power to block the project pending final judgment.
ladder.steelman: This is fundamentally a dispute over timing and authority rather than a final verdict: the Supreme Court cleared the way for construction to resume while the underlying legality of the waivers is still being litigated, meaning the physical and ecological changes on the ground could outpace — and complicate — whatever the courts ultimately decide about the law.
ladder.implications: Construction equipment and crews can now resume work in Big Bend National Park and along the broader 517-mile sector while Judge Cardone's court continues to weigh the legality of the waivers; any environmental or cultural-site alterations made during this period may be difficult to reverse even if the plaintiffs eventually prevail, and the case's final resolution could set a precedent for how broadly future administrations can invoke the 1996 waiver law in protected areas.

stories.headline: Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin
body: European officials will join U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi this week, France's foreign minister said Sunday, pushing back against the Kremlin's insistence that there could be no role for European powers at the meeting. "France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard," Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio, without specifying whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations or simply observe. The meetings, set for Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.

The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier ruled out a European role, saying the trilateral format had already been agreed. Speaking to a Russian news channel Friday, he accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them, while acknowledging that security talks would at some point require Europe's involvement. On Thursday, President Trump met Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and said a coming agreement was "going to involve more than Ukraine," adding it "might involve all of Europe."

This will be the fourth round of talks between the two warring nations brokered by the Trump administration, and the first since those in Geneva in February. Earlier U.S.-brokered meetings have made little progress. Moscow confirmed it would return to the negotiating table only after a visit by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg in October. Those talks saw Putin announce the release of an American prisoner from a Russian jail — an apparent Kremlin gesture to Trump's earlier lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports, a move Ukraine vehemently opposed. Witkoff has said the agenda for these latest talks will include postwar security arrangements, de-escalation of the conflict and humanitarian issues, shortly after Melania Trump helped broker a limited ceasefire that allowed humanitarian aid to enter a town inside Russian-occupied Ukraine.

Russia's delegation will again be led by hardline Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who has participated in most talks with Ukraine since March 2022. For the first time, the talks will also include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as Yury Zhigarlovsky, a deputy head of the General Staff's operations directorate, alongside military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov. The U.S. think tank Institute for the Study of War suggested some of those same Russian officials have previously sought to slow down previous talks or push harder on Moscow's demands. The gaps between the two countries remain substantial: Russia has demanded that Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted any security commitments should be clearly spelled out.

Zelenskyy told CNN on Friday that he had not been given details of the agreement Trump referenced, and warned: "For me, it's not simple, and it can be dangerous." He invoked the 1945 Yalta conference, where Allied leaders settled Europe's division without the involvement of several affected countries. The meetings in the United Arab Emirates also follow Democrats' midterm victories, which Zelenskyy said could improve Ukraine's chances of more U.S. aid. Russia, too, may be looking to push for the Trump administration's outlines of a Ukraine deal before a Democratic-controlled Congress arrives in January. Also hovering over the talks is the prospect of Trump, Xi and Putin gathering for a trilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China later this month; while details remain murky, all sides have confirmed discussions are underway.

As officials travel to Abu Dhabi to talk peace, the war has raged on regardless. Zelenskyy said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with only four intercepted, accusing Moscow of treating diplomacy "as a form of aggression." In southern Ukraine, the death toll from a guided-bomb strike Monday on an aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha rose to at least 55.

stories.headline: Explosion at Turkish steel plant kills at least 17
body: At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey, authorities said. The blast occurred around midday on Monday at the Habas Demir Celik plant in the Aliaga district, a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs. All those killed and injured were workers at the facility, one of the country's leading steel producers.

The local governor said the explosion happened after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a large industrial furnace below. Eyewitnesses said the blast shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air. The company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan originally said the death toll was 16, but later Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu announced that one of those who had been critically injured had died of their injuries, taking the toll to 17. Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble. Izmir Mayor Cemil Tugay said the full number of dead and injured would only become clear once the rubble had been cleared. At least five people have been arrested, according to local media reports cited by BBC News's Turkish service.

Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said. Workers' groups said there is a long record of safety issues at the factory. The Izmir chapter of Turkey's Labour Party said it was the third fatal incident at the factory in three weeks, and warned that seven employees had died in accidents at the plant in the past 10 years, adding that maintenance requirements and safety standards were not being met. Speaking after a cabinet meeting, Erdogan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued. The European Union and Azerbaijan were among those to send condolences.

stories.headline: Russia's leading independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta closes after eviction
body: Russia's leading independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, closed its Moscow office on Monday after being evicted from its premises and facing mounting state pressure, including being labeled a "foreign agent" by authorities. The team held a final editorial meeting before packing up and leaving, according to reports. The outlet, co-founded by former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev with funds from his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize, had been a flagship for post-Soviet democratic Russia and a persistent critic of the Kremlin.

The newspaper announced last month that it was being forced to shut down after being designated a "foreign agent" in September, a Soviet-era label revived by President Vladimir Putin's administration to stifle dissent. Following that designation, banks stopped processing the reader donations on which the paper relied for financial survival, especially after it moved wholly online following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Authorities also ordered the outlet to vacate its Moscow premises.

Nobel Peace Prize-winning co-founder Dmitry Muratov addressed journalists gathered to witness the closure. "Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today," he said, adding that constitutional guarantees for political and civil rights had "effectively ceased to function." Muratov called for a ceasefire in Ukraine, urged the release of around 4,000 people he termed political prisoners in Russia, and asked foreign observers to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people.

The Kremlin played down the closure. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia's media was highly diverse and that the newspaper's closure was part of "a standard rotational process" in a competitive landscape. United Nations human rights chief Volker Turk said in October that the closure was "yet another devastating blow for remaining independent media" in Russia.

Novaya Gazeta built a reputation for fearless investigative reporting into corruption, human rights violations, and abuse of power. Six of its journalists have been murdered since the paper was launched in 1993, including Anna Politkovskaya, who investigated abuses by Russia's military in Chechnya and was found dead in 2006. In recent months, authorities searched the home of editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov and took him for questioning, and another editor, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested in April. Sokolov said last month that the outlet had "been killed" by Russian authorities and special services.

It is not yet clear whether the closure in Moscow marks a definitive end to Novaya Gazeta's reporting or whether the outlet might seek to regroup and operate from outside Russia, as several other publications have been forced to do. One journalist, Irina Vorobyova, said the paper's spirit would survive like a "good virus" and would "continue in everyone that was part of it."

stories.headline: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO was target of Chinese spy
body: Nvidia has announced it is opening an independent investigation after reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang, was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The New York Times reported that US officials suspect Alice Huang, the managing director of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, of working for China's spy agency to collect intelligence. Nvidia said on Sunday that while it has no reason to believe that US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the inquiry will examine all available information. The company's board stated that it prioritises US national and economic security and has confidence in Jensen Huang and his leadership team.

The New York Times reported that Donald Trump was briefed last year on intelligence that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the Times reported, citing unnamed sources. China has denied the allegations, calling them 'entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China.'

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations, saying of Jensen Huang: 'I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.' Trump brushed off a question about whether he regrets not acting on the intelligence when briefed, and suggested he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. 'I haven't heard he's done anything wrong,' Trump said. 'He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.' Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia's security protocols and his relationship with Alice Huang.

Axios reported on Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full responsibility for his actions. 'I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,' Huang said in the draft email, also seen by Reuters. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report. Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, the company added.

The Times reported that a memo drafted by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia's chief executive was a spy for China's ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump's delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China's president.

Nvidia's powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang in one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. He has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development. National security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China. The investigation also follows a rough period on Wall Street for AI tech firms; a sell-off of tech stocks erased about $2tn in a month, with Nvidia's drop of 3.1% being the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward.

stories.headline: Jaguars acquire All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III from Falcons in multi-pick trade; Vikings urged to explore QB market
body: The Jacksonville Jaguars acquired All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III from the Atlanta Falcons on Monday, sending a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to Atlanta in exchange. Bates, 29, is in the final year of his contract and is expected to become a free agent at the end of the season, but the Jaguars have a history of extending players acquired in midseason trades, as they did with wide receiver Jakobi Meyers last year. The move bolsters a Jacksonville secondary that lost safety Eric Murray for the season to an elbow injury and comes as the Jaguars sit at 6-2 and eye a postseason push.

Bates entered the NFL as a second-round pick of the Cincinnati Bengals in 2018 out of Wake Forest. After five seasons in Cincinnati, he signed a four-year, $64.02 million contract with the Falcons in 2023. This season, Bates recorded one interception, three forced fumbles and 60 total tackles in nine games, while allowing a 78.3% completion percentage and a 115.2 passer rating in coverage, per TruMedia. He is tied for the second-most interceptions (28) in the NFL since entering the league and has been named a second-team All-Pro three times, including in 2025. He is also the only player in the past 40 years with at least 800 tackles and 25 interceptions before age 30.

Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski said Monday that the trade was not a signal of a sell-off, despite Atlanta falling to 3-6 after a loss to the Bengals in Madrid. “Obviously, we’re not where we want to be, we want to play better, but we’re very much in the thick of this thing and we trust in the guys that we have,” Stefanski said. “I understand the question, and I understand the question in light of the trade, but in no way, shape or form.” Stefanski named DeMarcco Hellams as Bates’s replacement at safety. Hellams, a seventh-round pick in 2023 out of Alabama, appeared in 15 games as a rookie but missed all of his second season after breaking his ankle during the preseason. Defensive back Sydney Brown is also expected to see increased reps.

CBS Sports graded the trade a B for the Jaguars, noting that two picks — especially a second-rounder in 2027 — is a steep price for a potential rental, but that Bates is one of the NFL’s best safeties and deepens a position group hit by injury. The Falcons received a B+, with analysts pointing out that Atlanta was likely to lose Bates in free agency anyway and that collecting a second-round pick is better than any compensatory pick they would have received. The trade is one of several moves reshaping rosters ahead of Tuesday’s 4 p.m. ET deadline. Other deals reported include defensive players Jeffery Simmons (Tennessee to Chicago), DeForest Buckner (Indianapolis to San Francisco) and Joey Porter Jr. (Pittsburgh to Dallas), as well as offensive skill players Jacoby Brissett (Arizona to Baltimore) and Marvin Harrison Jr. (Arizona to Houston).

Meanwhile, the Minnesota Vikings (6-1) are facing questions at quarterback. Carson Wentz will start Monday night against the Buffalo Bills after the team opted to bench Kyler Murray. ESPN’s Dan Orlovsky urged the Vikings to make “outrageous” trade calls if the offense continues to struggle. “If this offense looks pedestrian again, I just do not believe Minnesota can stand pat. I think anything is on the table at quarterback,” Orlovsky said on “The Pat McAfee Show.” “Even if it sounds outrageous to the NFL community, I think you have to start at, like, the most outrageous call you could make [for a] quarterback, and just work your way down the line.” Wentz has made two appearances this season, totaling 276 passing yards and three touchdowns while completing 59.0% of his passes; all three touchdowns came in a Week 1 win over the Packers.

stories.headline: Report details how Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum's Celtics partnership unraveled
body: The Boston Celtics stunned the NBA world this summer by trading Jaylen Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers in a deal that brought back Paul George, two first-round picks, and two second-round selections. Recent reporting, however, indicates that the trade was preceded by a quietly deteriorating relationship between Brown and the organization, as well as with fellow star Jayson Tatum.

Brown had arguably the best season of his career in 2025-26, finishing sixth in MVP voting, earning Second Team All-NBA honors, and averaging career highs of 28.7 points, 5.1 assists, and 6.9 rebounds per game. With Tatum limited to just 16 regular-season games while recovering from right Achilles tendon surgery, Brown stepped into the role of the Celtics' primary option. He believed his performance had elevated him to the same level as Tatum, but the front office apparently did not share that view.

According to King, Brown made it clear to the front office that he wanted to be treated more like a franchise player, on and off the court. After averaging 28.7 points per game, he felt he had reached a place in his career where he deserved the preferential treatment reserved for the game's premier players, including Tatum. The Celtics had previously asked Brown to sacrifice parts of his game for the team's benefit, a formula that helped Boston win the 2024 NBA title, with Brown earning Finals MVP after averaging 23.9 points, 5.9 rebounds, 3.3 assists, and 1.2 steals per game in the playoffs.

NBA Hall of Famer Tracy McGrady, a friend of Brown, commented on the situation, saying, 'I think his frustration lies deeply within the organization and other things that we don't really have the details to.' The reporting suggests that despite Brown's standout 2025-26 campaign, Boston continued to view Tatum as being on a level above Brown.

The 76ers went all-in this summer, adding Brown and LeBron James to a roster that already included Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe, and Joel Embiid. Philadelphia currently sits atop the Eastern Conference with a 9-2 record. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds, 4.0 assists, and 1.2 steals per game this season, with a usage rate of 25.9%—his lowest since the 2019-2020 campaign. For now, Brown appears content with his role, but the long-term dynamics of the star-laden 76ers lineup remain to be seen.

stories.headline: FDA orders class-wide label update for GLP-1 drugs over rare eye condition risk
body: The Food and Drug Administration on Monday ordered a labeling update for all approved GLP-1 receptor agonists to warn of a potential increased risk of a rare but serious eye condition called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION. The condition, sometimes described as an "eye stroke," is caused by insufficient blood flow to the optic nerve, typically leads to sudden vision loss, and can result in blindness; there are currently no proven treatments for it. The class-wide requirement covers 12 marketed drugs, including Novo Nordisk's semaglutide products Ozempic and Wegovy, as well as Eli Lilly's tirzepatide franchise Mounjaro, Zepbound, and the oral formulation Foundayo.

The FDA's action is based on an assessment launched after a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology found an association between Novo's semaglutide and a higher risk of NAION. The agency conducted a meta-analysis of 126 clinical trials across development programs. The analysis identified 15 probable NAION events: 10 in patients treated with GLP-1s, five in patients receiving placebo, and none in patients who received other non-GLP-1 glucose-lowering medication. This translated to a NAION incidence rate of 6.4 events per 100,000 patient-years for those treated with GLP-1s, compared with 3.8 events per 100,000 patient-years for comparators.

The FDA also examined real-world evidence through its data network, looking at NAION incidence among adults with type 2 diabetes. That study found no higher risk for NAION tied to GLP-1s compared with SGLT-2 inhibitors such as Boehringer Ingelheim and Eli Lilly's Jardiance, but did identify an increased risk when GLP-1s were compared with DPP-4 inhibitors such as Merck's Januvia. The regulator additionally reviewed reports of NAION among GLP-1 users from its adverse event monitoring system, but said those reports were difficult to interpret because risk factors for the disease often overlap with conditions commonly reported in patients treated with GLP-1s. An analysis of animal data failed to identify a mechanism for how GLP-1s could raise the potential risk of the eye condition.

The safety update comes as GLP-1 drugs have exploded in popularity for their potent weight loss effects, becoming some of the industry's top-selling products. Eli Lilly's tirzepatide brands Mounjaro and Zepbound generated a combined $36.51 billion in 2025, while Novo Nordisk's semaglutide franchise—Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus—brought in $36.19 billion over the same period. By comparison, Merck's PD-1 blockbuster Keytruda, which has amassed more than 40 indications, earned nearly $32 billion in 2025.

Analysts at BMO described the risk as limited for obesity drug coverage given the rarity of NAION incidence, noting that the FDA's action formalizes a previously recognized safety signal with low absolute event rates and amounts to a Warnings and Precautions update rather than a restriction on approved indications. The FDA's order requires pharmaceutical companies to inform patients and doctors of the potential risk through updated labeling.

stories.headline: NASA accelerates Moon landing plan to 2028 with competing landers
body: NASA has revealed an accelerated plan to return American astronauts to the Moon by 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and a crucial orbital test scheduled for 2027. The updated strategy, outlined by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman during an October 23 briefing, includes testing two lander systems, streamlining rocket preparations, and introducing a lighter spacesuit to help make the first moonwalks possible sooner. The plan builds on priorities introduced earlier this year through NASA's Ignition initiative and is intended to reduce technical risks, accelerate the schedule, and establish the foundation for a lasting American presence on the Moon.

Before attempting another crewed Moon landing, NASA plans to conduct a major rehearsal in Earth orbit. The Artemis III mission, scheduled for 2027, will bring together NASA's Orion spacecraft and experimental lunar landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin. Four astronauts will travel aboard Orion, launching on NASA's SLS rocket. During the planned 14-day mission, the crew will practice rendezvous and docking procedures with both companies' lander test vehicles. Blue Origin will first launch a test version of its Blue Moon lander into Earth orbit; Orion will then rendezvous and dock with it. Next, SpaceX will launch a test version of its Version 3 Starship lunar lander, and Orion will separate from Blue Moon and perform another docking with Starship. By testing both systems during a single crewed mission, NASA aims to gather essential operational experience before the 2028 landing attempt.

For Artemis IV in 2028, NASA intends to launch astronauts aboard Orion using the SLS rocket from Kennedy Space Center. Once in space, the crew will rely on a lunar landing system developed by either SpaceX or Blue Origin to reach the Moon's surface. SpaceX plans to use its Starship spacecraft, which will take on additional propellant while orbiting Earth before meeting Orion and carrying the spacecraft toward the Moon. Blue Origin is developing a different approach using its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, which would use additional propulsion stages in Earth orbit to send the lander toward the Moon before meeting Orion in lunar orbit. Both companies have revised their original mission designs to make operations simpler and more efficient. NASA is also considering two possible upper stages for the SLS rocket used on Artemis IV, preserving flexibility in its launch plans.

NASA is working with Axiom Space on a second, lighter spacesuit design known as the 'Sortie suit,' intended specifically for the first Moon surface excursions. The new suit weighs approximately half as much as Axiom's larger primary spacesuit, which could simplify preparations for the earliest landing missions and help astronauts begin exploring the lunar surface sooner. The lighter suit is not intended to replace the primary design, which will remain part of NASA's plans for future missions requiring longer periods outside the spacecraft and more demanding surface activities.

NASA has also reported significant progress in hardware preparation. Improvements in processing have reduced preparation timelines by approximately 50%, and NASA engineers redesigned, manufactured, and tested a critical rocket fuel-line component in just five months at roughly one-tenth of an earlier estimate from an external vendor. 'NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it,' said Jeremy Parsons, the agency's Artemis program manager. The improvements reflect NASA's broader effort to strengthen its internal engineering capabilities and shorten development schedules.

NASA's ambitions extend beyond returning astronauts to the lunar surface for a single mission. The agency intends to send crews on increasingly challenging expeditions near the Moon's South Pole, with the goal of establishing an enduring human presence on the Moon. The experience gained from these missions will also help NASA prepare for sending the first astronauts to Mars. In a separate development, NASA is also accepting applications for new astronauts, with a starting salary of $164,395 and applications accepted through Dec. 3. The agency is seeking candidates to live and work on the Moon in a future moon base, with requirements including a master's degree in a STEM-related field—now including nursing degrees—and three years of related professional experience.

stories.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits affair with alleged Chinese spy; board opens investigation
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes was working as a spy for China, prompting the company's board to open an independent investigation. In an internal message to employees on Sunday obtained by the Financial Times, Huang apologized for being unfaithful to his wife, saying, "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Nvidia said its board would investigate "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." Huang said he would fully cooperate.

The Financial Times reported Friday that U.S. officials believe Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker. American officials this year wrote a memo, based on intelligence, that described the relationship, according to people familiar with the document. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence Nvidia's efforts to loosen chip export restrictions. A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations as "groundless smears and slanders." No one has been charged.

The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia, which has been at the center of the AI boom. Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to expand access to China, calling export controls a "failure" and warning that shutting Nvidia out of China's market would enable the country to develop its own AI chips. In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue. The affair has already led Huang to pull out of speaking engagements, including the ElevenLabs Summit and the Anthropic CEO Forum.

The incident has rattled the AI industry and raised questions about Huang's future as CEO. Yale leadership professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimated Huang's chances of survival at "about a 50-50," noting that while Huang has earned considerable goodwill since co-founding Nvidia in 1993, the recklessness of the situation could lead to an "irretrievable loss of confidence." Unlike other executives who survived personal scandals, Huang has no obvious successor at Nvidia, where he maintains roughly 60 direct reports and a flat structure. The board's independent members are expected to examine what technology may have reached China and Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, which bought roughly $2 billion of Nvidia's chips and has faced questions about whether it helped China circumvent U.S. export restrictions.

stories.headline: Anthropic Releases Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 With Faster, Cheaper AI and Claims of Solving Physics Problems
body: Anthropic announced the release of two new AI models on Monday: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2. The company says the models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, and can generate outputs faster than their 5.1 predecessors, which were released in September. Claude Fable 5.2 is available to the public starting today, while access to Claude Mythos 5.2 is limited to vetted organizations.

Anthropic claims that during prerelease testing, the models "helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours." The company also says Fable 5.2 is designed to tackle challenging software engineering problems, orchestrate agent teams, and handle long-running projects. The new model is priced at $8 per million input tokens, down from $10 for the previous version, making it cheaper than its primary competitor, GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says the new Fable returns responses 30% faster across effort levels, with faster inference serving available for double the price. Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system.

The release is Anthropic's first since a third-party report from the assessment group METR suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI), or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found that internal models were speeding up Anthropic's AI progress by roughly 2x, though many uncertainties remain. Anthropic's release notes acknowledge ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities, stating: "Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow."

Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a conclusion detailed in Mythos 5.2's system card. The system card notes that "Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor," but adds that "low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations."

Separately, AI startup Physical Superintelligence (PSI) announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. PSI said the result was achieved by running "a non-public Anthropic model" within its own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model used.
